zebralogic.title: Interpret adjacency and ordering clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: When a clue uses terms like 'directly left of', 'directly right of', or similar, enforce that the two houses are adjacent with the specified direction.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue mentions direct adjacency or ordering with direction.
zebralogic.example: Treating 'directly left of' as merely 'somewhere left of', allowing non‑adjacent placements.

zebralogic.title: Interpret distance clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: When a clue says 'N houses between X and Y', enforce that there are exactly N houses separating X and Y (i.e., |pos(X)‑pos(Y)| = N+1).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue mentions a specific number of houses between two items.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting 'one house between X and Y' as X and Y being adjacent (distance 1) instead of distance 2.

zebralogic.title: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality
zebralogic.principle: Interpret 'X is somewhere left of Y' (or right of) as a strict ordering constraint pos(X) < pos(Y) (or >) without requiring adjacency.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses the phrasing 'somewhere left of' or 'somewhere right of'.
zebralogic.example: Assuming X must be directly adjacent to Y when the clue only says 'somewhere left of'.

zebralogic.title: Apply exclusion constraints
zebralogic.principle: If a clue explicitly forbids an attribute from a particular house (e.g., 'X is not in house 2'), enforce that X cannot occupy that house and propagate uniqueness.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue contains a negative placement.
zebralogic.example: Ignoring a clue that says 'Bob is not in house 3' and placing Bob there.

zebralogic.title: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category
zebralogic.principle: Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; no two houses can share the same attribute value.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Throughout solving; after any assignment, ensure the same value cannot be assigned elsewhere.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the same car model to two different houses.

zebralogic.title: Preserve original case of attribute values
zebralogic.principle: When outputting the final grid, copy each attribute value exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving its case.
zebralogic.example: Changing 'British' to 'british' or otherwise altering capitalization.

zebralogic.title: Interpret 'next to each other' as adjacency
zebralogic.principle: When a clue says two items are 'next to each other', enforce that their house positions differ by exactly one, without specifying direction.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses the phrase 'next to each other' or similar.
zebralogic.example: Treating 'next to each other' as any ordering, allowing a gap between the two items.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for name-attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly links a specific name to an attribute (e.g., 'Alice is the doctor'), enforce that the name has that attribute and that attribute belongs exclusively to that name.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue states a name‑attribute relationship.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the attribute to the named person but not preventing another person from also having that attribute.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for attribute-attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue links two non‑name attributes (e.g., 'The Norwegian uses a Samsung'), enforce that they co‑occur in the same house, i.e., both attributes belong to the same entity.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue states a relationship between two attributes.
zebralogic.example: Treating 'The Norwegian uses a Samsung' as only a one‑way implication, allowing the Samsung user to be non‑Norwegian.

zebralogic.title: Apply direct placement constraints
zebralogic.principle: When a clue explicitly places an attribute in a specific house (e.g., 'The cat is in house 2'), enforce that the attribute occupies that house and that no other house can have that attribute.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue contains a positive house assignment.
zebralogic.example: Ignoring a clue that says 'The cat is in house 2' and placing the cat elsewhere.

zebralogic.description: Interpreting 'N houses between' as distance N
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model confuses the number of houses separating two items with the total positional distance, forgetting that 'N houses between' means there are N houses in between, so the positions differ by N+1.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: When parsing such clues, add 1 to the given number to compute the positional distance, i.e., enforce |pos(X) - pos(Y)| = N + 1.

zebralogic.description: Ignoring equivalence clues that bind two attributes to the same house
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model treats the clue as a one‑way implication, not enforcing that both attributes must co‑occur in the same house.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Treat any clue linking two attributes as a bidirectional equivalence, ensuring both attributes are assigned to the same house.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model may assign the same attribute value to multiple houses, overlooking the global uniqueness constraint.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: After each assignment, enforce that each attribute value appears exactly once across all houses.

zebralogic.description: Altering attribute values (spelling/casing) instead of copying them verbatim
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalises or changes the case of attribute strings during generation, deviating from the exact tokens given in the problem.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute tokens exactly as they appear in the problem statement, preserving case, spelling, and any abbreviations.
